### Detail

When two requests simultaneously save rich text content for the same record and attribute, both build a new `ActionText::RichText` in memory and attempt to `INSERT` it on the parent save. The database unique index on `(record_type, record_id, name)` guarantees that only one succeeds; the loser raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`.

items.title: `ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!` leaks an orphaned `raw_email` blob on every duplicate delivery
items.body:
`create_and_extract_message_id!` dedupes re-delivered inbound emails by rescuing `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` (the unique index on `[message_id, message_checksum]`). But the raw-email blob is created **and uploaded** as an argument that is evaluated *before* the `create!` that fails — and nothing cleans it up on the rescue path.

### Steps to reproduce

```ruby
source = <<~EMAIL
  Message-ID: <dup@example.com>
  From: a@example.com
  To: b@example.com
  Subject: hello

  body
EMAIL

# First delivery: creates the InboundEmail + its raw_email blob (expected)
ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!(source)

before = ActiveStorage::Blob.count
# Second (duplicate) delivery: returns nil via the RecordNotUnique rescue
ActionMailbox::InboundEmail.create_and_extract_message_id!(source)
after = ActiveStorage::Blob.count

after - before # => 1   (an orphaned, unattached blob — and its bytes were uploaded to the service)
```

https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/fa670164ca2cc821e0016acece42e0bb6bbb27e8/actionmailbox/app/models/action_mailbox/inbound_email/message_id.rb#L20 creates + uploads the blob, then the `rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` rolls back the `InboundEmail` creation, but leaves the blob.

### Expected behavior

A duplicate delivery is a clean no-op that creates no new `ActiveStorage::Blob` and uploads nothing to the storage service.

### Actual behavior

Each duplicate delivery leaves a fully-uploaded, unreferenced `message/rfc822` blob:

- `create_and_upload_raw_email!` runs first (argument evaluation), committing the blob row and uploading the bytes to the service.
- `create!` then violates the `[message_id, message_checksum]` unique index and raises `RecordNotUnique`, which is rescued to `nil`.
- There's no transaction wrapping the method, so the blob row is already committed; and the storage upload isn't transactional, so even a wrapping transaction wouldn't remove the object. The blob is orphaned with no attachment and no owning record.

Duplicate deliveries are common in practice (ingress providers such as Postmark/Mailgun retry/redeliver), so this accumulates. In one production app we found ~1,900 orphaned `raw_email` blobs (~27 GB) plus an ongoing trickle proportional to the duplicate-delivery rate — invisible to error tracking because the exception is intentionally swallowed.

### Proposed fix

Preferably avoid the wasted upload entirely by short-circuiting on an existing record before uploading:

```ruby
def create_and_extract_message_id!(source, **options)
  message_checksum = OpenSSL::Digest::SHA1.hexdigest(source)
  message_id = extract_message_id(source) || generate_missing_message_id(message_checksum)

  return if exists?(message_id: message_id, message_checksum: message_checksum)

  create! raw_email: create_and_upload_raw_email!(source),
    message_id: message_id, message_checksum: message_checksum, **options
rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
  nil
end
```

This still keeps the `rescue` as a race-safe backstop — but on the backstop path the just-created blob should be purged (e.g. capture the blob, and `blob&.purge` in the rescue) so the race case doesn't leak either.

Happy to submit a PR with this fix.

### System configuration

**Rails version:** reproduces on `main`; present in 8.1.3 and earlier.
**Ruby version:** 4.0.5

items.body:
Hi All,
I think for the following configuration  accepts_nested_attributes_for + validation seems to be broken!!
Rails 4.2.1
Ruby 2.1.3

```
class Country < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :cities, dependent: :destroy
  accepts_nested_attributes_for :cities
end

class City < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :country
  validates :language , uniqueness: { scope: :country_id }
end

country = Country.new(description:'abc', language: 'en-US', cities:[City.new(language: 'en-US', text: 'abc'), City.new(language: 'en-US', text: 'abc')])

works!!

```

items.title: Fix create_or_find_by duplicating WHERE conditions on retry within transaction
items.body:
When `create_or_find_by` rescues a `RecordNotUnique` inside a transaction, the previous `where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes)` applied the attributes twice — and if the relation already had conflicting scope conditions for the same key, the generated SQL would be contradictory (e.g. `WHERE nick = 'irvan' AND nick = 'bob'`), raising `RecordNotFound`.

Fix by using `rewhere(attributes).lock.take!` instead: `rewhere` replaces existing conditions for those attribute keys rather than stacking them, and `take!` fetches the record without adding further WHERE clauses.

Fixes #57192

<!--
Thanks for contributing to Rails!

Please do not make *Draft* pull requests, as they still send
notifications to everyone watching the Rails repo.

Create a pull request when it is ready for review and feedback
from the Rails team :).

If your pull request affects documentation or any non-code
changes, guidelines for those changes are [available
here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#contributing-to-the-rails-documentation)

About this template

The following template aims to help contributors write a good description for their pull requests.
We'd like you to provide a description of the changes in your pull request (i.e. bugs fixed or features added), the motivation behind the changes, and complete the checklist below before opening a pull request.

Feel free to discard it if you need to (e.g. when you just fix a typo). -->

### Motivation / Background

`create_or_find_by` raises `RecordNotFound` when called on a scoped relation
inside a transaction. When rescuing `RecordNotUnique`, the previous code used
`where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes)`, which applied the lookup
attributes twice on top of the existing scope. If the scope already had a
condition for the same key with a different value, the SQL became contradictory:

```sql
-- Subscriber.where(nick: "irvan").create_or_find_by(nick: "bob") inside a transaction
WHERE nick = 'irvan' AND nick = 'bob' AND nick = 'bob'
```

This always returns zero rows, raising `RecordNotFound` instead of the existing record.

### Detail

Replaced `where(attributes).lock.find_by!(attributes)` with
`rewhere(attributes).lock.take!` in the transactional rescue branch of both
`create_or_find_by` and `create_or_find_by!`.

`rewhere` removes any existing scope conditions for the specified attribute
keys before applying the new ones, preventing conflicting duplicates.
`take!` then fetches the first matching record without appending further
WHERE clauses.

### Checklist

* [x] This Pull Request is related to one change.
* [x] Commit message has a detailed description of what changed and why. Fixes #57192
* [x] Tests are added or updated if you fix a bug or add a feature.
* [x] CHANGELOG updated in activerecord.

items.title: New find_or_create_by behavior in Rails 7.1 can introduce subtransactions in PostgreSQL
items.body:
In https://github.com/rails/rails/pull/45720, `find_or_create_by` was modified to call `create_or_find_by`, but that [method](https://github.com/rails/rails/blob/023a3eb3c046091a5d52027393a6d29d0576da01/activerecord/lib/active_record/relation.rb#L214-L218) can introduce subtransactions in PostgreSQL via the `transaction(requires_new: true)` call:

```ruby
def create_or_find_by(attributes, &block)
  transaction(requires_new: true) { create(attributes, &block) }
rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
  find_by!(attributes)
end
```

As I mentioned in https://about.gitlab.com/blog/2021/09/29/why-we-spent-the-last-month-eliminating-postgresql-subtransactions/, we spent a lot of effort to get rid of subtransactions because they suffer from significant performance issues at scale. We saw all our database replicas stall out at times as a result:

> In a busy database, it's possible for the size of the subtransaction log to grow so large that the working set no longer fits into memory. This results in a lot of cache misses, which in turn causes a high amount of disk I/O and CPU as PostgreSQL furiously tries to load data from disk to keep up with all the lookups.

Has this been solved in PostgreSQL yet? No. The commits highlighted in https://postgres.ai/blog/20210831-postgresql-subtransactions-considered-harmful#ideas-for-postgresql-development haven't made it into PostgreSQL upstream yet. I see there is recent activity in this thread: https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/flat/CAFiTN-vzDvNz=ExGXz6gdyjtzGixKSqs0mKHMmaQ8sOSEFZ33A@mail.gmail.com

For now, we're going to patch ActiveRecord to revert the change, but I'd suggest reverting this or making it some option for those who really need to deal with the racy conditions outlined.

items.body:
### Steps to reproduce

here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#creating-a-bug-report)) -->

<!-- Paste your executable test case created from one of the scripts found [here](https://edgeguides.rubyonrails.org/contributing_to_ruby_on_rails.html#create-an-executable-test-case) below: -->
```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  git_source(:github) { |repo| "https://github.com/#{repo}.git" }
  	
  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "7-1-stable"
  # Switch to below works
  # gem "rails", github: "rails/rails", branch: "7-0-stable"
  gem "mysql2"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

opts = {
  database: "unique_keys_test",
  adapter: "mysql2",
  username: "root"
}
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(opts.except(:database))
ActiveRecord::Base.connection.drop_database(opts[:database])
ActiveRecord::Base.connection.create_database(opts[:database])
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(opts)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :tags, force: true do |t|
    t.string :foo
    t.bigint :foo_id
    t.string :name
    t.index [:foo, :foo_id], unique: true
  end
end

class Tag < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_find_or_create_by
    2.times do |t|
      begin
        Tag.find_or_create_by!(foo: 'Foo', foo_id: 1, name: "foo_#{t}")
      rescue ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique
        # some app logic that handles RecordNotUnique
      end
    end

    assert_equal 1, Tag.count
  end
end

```

### Expected behavior
This is almost the same as https://github.com/rails/rails/issues/48035 but without concurrency involved.

In Rails 7.0, `find_or_create_by!` with duplicated uniqueness constraints raises `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` error

items.title: Using `create_or_find_by` led to primary keys running out
items.body:
### Steps to reproduce
While this doesn't fully assert the issue, it shows that the primary key can grow tremendously without actually writing new rows.

```ruby
# frozen_string_literal: true

require "bundler/inline"

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"

  git_source(:github) { |repo| "https://github.com/#{repo}.git" }

  gem "rails", github: "rails/rails"
  gem "pg"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "postgresql", database: "rails")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do
  create_table :posts, force: true do |t|
  end

  create_table :comments, force: true do |t|
    t.integer :post_id
  end

  add_index :comments, :post_id, unique: true
end

class Post < ActiveRecord::Base
  has_many :comments
end

class Comment < ActiveRecord::Base
  belongs_to :post
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test

  # PROBLEM
  # When create fails, the autoincremented id does not roll back
  def test_primary_key_growth
    post_one = Post.create!

    comment_for_post_one = Comment.create_or_find_by(post: post_one)

    # Create fails for Post 1's second comment and it finds the same record for
    # first_comment_for_post_one
    1000.times do
      second_comment_for_post_one = Comment.create_or_find_by(post: post_one)
      assert_equal second_comment_for_post_one, comment_for_post_one
    end

    post_two = Post.create!
    # This fails
    # Failure:
    #   BugTest#test_primary_key_growth [create_or_find_by.rb:56]:
    #   Expected: 2
    #     Actual: #<Comment id: 1002, post_id: 2>
    comment_for_post_two = Comment.create_or_find_by(post: post_two)
    assert_equal comment_for_post_one.id + 1, comment_for_post_two.id
  end

   # This is nothing new, as the same thing can happen with `create`
  def test_create
    post_one = Post.create!

    comment_for_post_one = Comment.create(post: post_one)

    1000.times do
      assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique do
        second_comment_for_post_one = Comment.create(post: post_one)
      end
    end

    post_two = Post.create!
    comment_for_post_two = Comment.create(post: post_two)
    assert_equal comment_for_post_one.id + 1, comment_for_post_two.id
  end
end
```

### Problem
Each time `create_or_find_by` hits `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique`, it rolls back, but the auto-increment does not. [The fact that auto-increment does not roll back seems to be expected behavior from PostgreSQL](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/20040420005747.GA19205%40wolff.to).

Still, the fact that this happens with `create_or_find_by` **led to one of our database tables running out of primary keys in production**, preventing the creation of any new rows.

### System configuration
**Rails version**:
6.0

**Ruby version**:
2.5.3

items.title: Inconsistent behavior between save and save! when unsetting object.id on a new record
items.body:
If you make a new model object `foo` and manually set `foo.id` to a value that's already in use, then call `foo.save` or `foo.save!`, you'll get an `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` error (as expected).

However, if you then set `foo.id = nil` and call `foo.save!`, you'll get _another_ `ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique` error. The SQL statements will show that Rails still uses the `id` from before.

On the other hand, if you set `foo.id = nil` and call `foo.save`, the record is saved with an automatically assigned `id` as expected.

Test case:

```ruby
begin
  require "bundler/inline"
rescue LoadError => e
  $stderr.puts "Bundler version 1.10 or later is required. Please update your Bundler"
  raise e
end

gemfile(true) do
  source "https://rubygems.org"
  gem "rails", '5.0.2'
  gem "sqlite3"
end

require "active_record"
require "minitest/autorun"
require "logger"

# This connection will do for database-independent bug reports.
ActiveRecord::Base.establish_connection(adapter: "sqlite3", database: ":memory:")
ActiveRecord::Base.logger = Logger.new(STDOUT)

ActiveRecord::Schema.define do

  create_table "foos", force: :cascade do |t|
    t.string "name"
  end

end

class Foo < ActiveRecord::Base
end

class BugTest < Minitest::Test
  def test_save_with_duplicate_id
    foo = Foo.create(name: "Original")
    dup_foo = Foo.new(name: "Duplicate", id: foo.id)

    assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique do
      dup_foo.save
    end

    dup_foo.id = nil

    assert_nil dup_foo.id

    dup_foo.save

    refute_equal dup_foo.id, foo.id
  end

  def test_save_bang_with_duplicate_id
    foo = Foo.create(name: "Original")
    dup_foo = Foo.new(name: "Duplicate", id: foo.id)

    assert_raises ActiveRecord::RecordNotUnique do
      dup_foo.save!
    end

    dup_foo.id = nil

    assert_nil dup_foo.id

    dup_foo.save!                    # Exception happens here

    refute_equal dup_foo.id, foo.id  # If the second exception is rescued, this assertion fails.
  end
end
```

The first test passes, but the second one fails.

This behavior happens on Rails 5.0.2 and on 5.1.0.beta1.
